component.name: Apache Knox
component.description: Application gateway / reverse proxy providing perimeter security for the REST APIs and web UIs of Hadoop-ecosystem (and other) services. A long-running Jetty-based edge daemon terminates client TLS, authenticates callers through a configurable provider chain (LDAP/AD via Shiro, Kerberos, SAML/OIDC/CAS via pac4j, header pre-auth, SSO cookie, JWT), authorizes against service-level ACLs, rewrites URLs to hide internal topology, dispatches requests to backends while asserting the caller's identity, issues KnoxSSO and KnoxToken tokens, and manages secrets in a master-secret-protected credential store. Knox's whole purpose is to be a trust boundary.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it. The source is a v0 draft by the ASF Security team with the Knox PMC chair's line-by-line review of 2026-07-09 folded in.

blueprints.name: Knox gateway deployment
blueprints.description: North of Knox: untrusted HTTP/WebSocket clients at the perimeter. South of Knox: trusted backend cluster services and the federated IdP. Per request: TLS termination, then the topology-defined provider chain (authentication, identity assertion, authorization, rewrite, dispatch); identity assertion is the trust-elevation point after which the request carries Knox-minted identity the backend trusts.

assets.name: Knox gateway request pipeline
assets.description: Jetty-based routing and filter chain, provider chain (authentication, identity assertion, authorization), rewrite/URL translation, and dispatch/proxy to backends.

assets.name: KnoxSSO and KnoxToken services
assets.description: The /knoxsso and /knoxtoken endpoints issuing signed, short-TTL, revocation-optional bearer tokens and SSO cookies.

assets.name: Master secret and credential stores
assets.description: Master-secret-protected credential store / alias service and keystores under data/security/, protected by OS filesystem permissions; -persist-master trades a prompt for on-disk storage and requires careful file permission management.

assets.name: Backend cluster services
assets.description: The Hadoop services Knox fronts (WebHDFS, YARN, HBase, Hive, etc.); trusted to enforce their own authorization once Knox asserts identity.

assets.name: Federated identity provider
assets.description: LDAP/AD, SAML/OIDC provider that Knox delegates authentication to; authoritative and honest, with assertions integrity-protected in transit (signed SAML, validated OIDC ID token, LDAPS).

zones.name: Perimeter clients
zones.description: Untrusted HTTP/WebSocket peers reaching the gateway listen port; the primary adversary.

zones.name: Knox gateway
zones.description: The gateway daemon, its provider chain, token services, and filesystem-protected secrets, operated by a trusted cluster administrator.

zones.name: Trusted cluster and IdP
zones.description: Backend services and the federated IdP on the far side of the boundary; clients are assumed unable to reach backends except through Knox (operator network segmentation).

persona.description: Untrusted HTTP/WebSocket peer: sends arbitrary request lines, headers (including spoofed identity/forwarded headers), bodies, and frames; presents forged or replayed credentials, cookies, SAML responses, OIDC tokens, and KnoxTokens. A secondary variant holds valid credentials for some topology and tries to exceed them.

Authors topology descriptors and provider configs and manages the master secret and keystores; trusted for the instance, out of scope as an adversary (malicious operator config is never a Knox vulnerability).
Trusted infrastructure on the far side of the boundary; Knox trusts IdP assertions and trusts backends to enforce their own authorization.

assumptions.description: The filesystem is the operator trust anchor: only the operator and the Knox process user can read the master secret file, credential stores, and identity keystore.
The backend trusts Knox's asserted identity, so anything that lets a client control the asserted identity is an authentication bypass against every backend.
TLS to the backend is assumed required, in particular to protect SPNEGO tokens forwarded on the dispatch hop; TLS is required together with Kerberos for proxy-user-based trusted proxies.
Clustered Knox instances share the same gateway master secret and are mutually trusting, not adversarial to each other.

threats.name: Perimeter authentication bypass
threats.description: An unauthenticated client reaches a protected backend or gets a response it should not, despite a correctly configured topology with an authentication provider. A request failing authentication or authorization never reaches dispatch, with no exceptions; a bypass is security-critical.

threats.name: Identity assertion forgery (impersonation to the backend)
threats.description: A client substitutes another principal so that the identity Knox asserts to the backend (doAs/proxy-user header, SPNEGO) is not the one Knox authenticated. Faithful identity assertion is the keystone property; any break is security-critical, because the backend trusts Knox-minted identity.

threats.name: Authorization bypass or cross-topology escape
threats.description: An authenticated-but-limited client reaches a service or topology it is not authorized for (topology ACL bypass, cross-topology confusion, rewrite escape into other topologies/services). Isolation between topologies is proposed as operator partitioning rather than a Knox-enforced boundary; a cross-topology leak is valid only if it breaks the authentication or authorization enforcement properties.

threats.name: KnoxToken/KnoxSSO forgery or tampering
threats.description: A client mints, forges, tampers with, or gets an expired token accepted without the corresponding credential. Tokens are integrity-protected (signed) and validated (signature plus expiry, plus server-side revocation where applicable) before acceptance; a violation is security-critical.

threats.name: Bearer token replay within TTL
threats.description: KnoxSSO cookies and KnoxTokens are bearer credentials, not proof of possession: anyone who captures one can replay it until expiry. Replay within TTL is by design; TLS, short TTLs, and (where available) revocation are load-bearing, not decorative.

threats.name: Network disclosure of stored secrets
threats.description: A network request discloses an alias, a provider secret, or the master secret. Master-secret-encrypted credential stores protect secrets at rest and secrets are not exposed over the network surface; a network-reachable disclosure is security-critical, while anything requiring local filesystem access is the operator boundary.

threats.name: Topology and internal-address disclosure
threats.description: A client obtains internal backend host/port addresses or reaches an un-fronted internal endpoint via a rewrite escape, defeating the stated topology-concealment purpose. Concealment is obscurity, not an access control; generic stack traces are at most hardening, real internal-address leaks defeat the property.

threats.name: Reverse-proxy attack classes (smuggling, SSRF, open redirect, XXE, header confusion)
threats.description: As a reverse proxy Knox is exposed to HTTP request smuggling/desync between Knox and backend, SSRF via rewrite/dispatch if client input reaches the backend target, open redirect via the SSO originalUrl/return-URL parameter, XXE in providers parsing attacker-supplied XML (e.g. SAML responses), host-header and X-Forwarded-* trust confusion, WebSocket origin/authorization gaps, and KnoxSSO cookie scope/Secure/HttpOnly handling. Knox provides the mechanisms (WebAppSecProvider for XSRF/CORS/CSP; regexp whitelists for SSRF/open-redirect) but tuning them is the operator's responsibility: a protection that is available but unconfigured is out of model, a bypass of a configured protection is valid.

threats.name: Gateway crash or hang from unauthenticated input
threats.description: The confirmed resource line: an unauthenticated request that hangs or crashes the gateway process is a bug; merely consuming proportionate resources under load is not. Knox makes no strong quantitative resource guarantee beyond Jetty/topology limits; slow-loris, large-body, and many-connection pressure are bounded by operator configuration.

threats.name: Ungated HeaderPreAuth trusts client-supplied identity headers
threats.description: HeaderPreAuth (SM_USER and custom identity headers) looks like it authenticates the user but only trusts a header; it is secure only when paired with an mTLS/IP trust gate proving the header came from a trusted SSO front-end. Without the gate any client can impersonate anyone; the most dangerous Knox false friend. Per the PMC, an ungated deployment is the operator's risk to accept (out of model, non-default configuration), not a Knox bug, with a standing hardening ask that Knox default the trust gate.

threats.name: Findings requiring the demo/sample surface
threats.description: The bundled demo LDAP (ApacheDS), sample sandbox topology, gateway sample apps, and self-signed test certificate are explicitly for evaluation, not production; findings that only manifest with them in use are out of model as unsupported components.

threats.name: Bypassing Knox by reaching the backend directly
threats.description: Knox is a perimeter control and does not defend a backend that is directly network-reachable around the gateway; network segmentation is the operator's responsibility. Clients able to authenticate directly to the backend (e.g. via Kerberos) are a legitimate deployment choice, and without explicit proxy-user configuration they cannot assert another user's identity via doAs.

threats.name: Plaintext or unverified backend dispatch hop
threats.description: TLS termination at Knox does not encrypt the gateway-to-backend hop; that hop's encryption and hostname verification are separate operator configuration, and a plaintext/unverified hop is a misuse pattern, not a Knox guarantee. TLS on this hop is required to protect forwarded SPNEGO tokens.

trustBoundaries.name: Perimeter trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Untrusted clients meet the gate where a request is authenticated, authorized, and only then re-emitted as trusted. Client-supplied identity headers and tokens are the crown-jewel untrusted inputs; the most consequential failure class is a client getting Knox to assert an identity it did not legitimately earn.

trustBoundaries.name: Dispatch trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: After identity assertion the request carries Knox-minted identity that the backend trusts; the dispatch hop opens a (possibly new-TLS) connection to the backend, whose encryption and verification are operator-configured.

controls.name: Topology-ordered provider chain enforcement
controls.description: The provider chain runs in topology-defined order (authentication, identity assertion, authorization, rewrite, dispatch); a request failing authentication or authorization never reaches dispatch, and the asserted identity is the one Knox authenticated.

controls.name: Service-level ACL authorization (AclsAuthz)
controls.description: Given an authorization provider, only principals/groups/IPs permitted by the topology ACL reach the service; perimeter ACLs are coarse and do not replace backend/Ranger fine-grained authorization.

controls.name: Signed, validated KnoxSSO/KnoxToken tokens
controls.description: Tokens and SSO cookies are signed and validated (signature, expiry, and server-side revocation where applicable) before acceptance.

controls.name: Short token TTLs and revocation
controls.description: Set token TTLs and enable server-managed revocation appropriate to data sensitivity; a captured bearer token is replayable until expiry, so TTL and revocation are load-bearing.

controls.name: Master-secret-protected credential stores
controls.description: Provider and gateway secrets are held in master-secret-encrypted credential stores (per-gateway and per-topology .jceks) behind the alias service, not exposed over the network surface.

controls.name: Protect the master secret and keystores on disk
controls.description: Protect the master secret file, credential stores, and identity keystore with OS file permissions; treat -persist-master as security-sensitive (it trades a prompt for on-disk storage and requires careful file permission management).

controls.name: Configure WebAppSecProvider (XSRF, CORS, CSP)
controls.description: The WebAppSecProvider can be configured for XSRF, CORS, CSP, and related cross-site protections; Knox provides the mechanism, the operator must turn it on and tune it to the deployment.

controls.name: Regexp whitelists against SSRF and open redirect
controls.description: Regexp-based whitelists (allowed hosts, ports, domains) protect against SSRF and open redirect via the SSO return-URL; they must be tuned to the deployment's specific expectations. Dispatch targets otherwise come from trusted topology descriptors, not client input.

controls.name: Pair HeaderPreAuth with an mTLS/IP trust gate
controls.description: Never deploy HeaderPreAuth without a trust gate (mTLS or IP allow-list proving the identity header comes from a trusted SSO front-end); the PMC's standing hardening ask is that Knox default the gate so operators must explicitly accept the ungated posture.

controls.name: TLS on the backend dispatch hop
controls.description: Configure the dispatch hop's TLS protocol, ciphers, and hostname verification to match the threat environment; TLS is required together with Kerberos for proxy-user-based trusted proxies because it protects the forwarded SPNEGO tokens.

controls.name: Network segmentation so backends are unreachable except through Knox
controls.description: Knox assumes clients cannot reach backends except through it but does not enforce this; the operator's network must.

controls.name: Replace all demo/sample material before production
controls.description: Remove the demo LDAP, sample sandbox topology, and self-signed certificate; install a real IdP and a CA-issued identity keystore, keeping provider configs pointed at integrity-checked IdP channels (signed SAML, validated OIDC, LDAPS).

controls.name: URL rewriting conceals cluster topology
controls.description: Per-service rewrite rules translate external URLs to internal ones and back, hiding backend host/port layout behind a single Knox endpoint; concealment reduces attack surface but is not itself an authentication or authorization boundary.
